title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable, Navigable, and Editable
hook: An agent is only as good as its harness — the code that builds prompts, manages state, calls tools. The real bottleneck isn't editing that code, it's finding where a behavior lives in a huge codebase.
key_points: An agent's capability depends as much on its harness (prompting, state, tool invocation, execution coordination) as on the foundation model underneath it.
Harnesses evolve constantly, but finding every code location that implements a target behavior is hard — production harnesses are large, tightly coupled, and behaviorally distributed.
Introduces the Harness Handbook: a behavior-centric map synthesized automatically via static analysis plus LLM-assisted structuring, linking each behavior to its source code.
Pairs it with Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD), which walks agents from high-level behaviors down to implementation details and verifies candidate locations against current source.

On modification requests across two open-source harnesses, Handbook-assisted planning improves localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens — largest gains on scattered, rarely-run, or cross-module behaviors.
content_html: An AI agent's capability comes from two things: its foundation model, and its harness — the surrounding code that builds prompts, tracks state, invokes tools, and coordinates execution. Harnesses have to keep changing as models, APIs, and requirements evolve, but this paper zeroes in on a step that happens before any edit: figuring out where in a large, tightly-coupled codebase a given behavior actually lives.
extra_html:
Ruhan Wang and colleagues call this behavior localization, and argue it's a central bottleneck in harness evolution — code search and long-context reading still leave the mapping from "what the system should do" to "which files implement it" for a human or agent to reconstruct by hand. Their fix is the Harness Handbook: a behavior-centric representation built automatically from a harness codebase via static analysis and LLM-assisted structuring, which links each behavior directly to its implementing source. Alongside it, Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD) walks an agent from high-level behaviors down to relevant implementation details, checking candidate locations against the current source as it goes.

Tested on real modification requests against two open-source harnesses, Handbook-assisted planning improves both localization accuracy and edit-plan quality while spending fewer planner tokens — with the biggest wins on behaviors that are scattered across files, rarely exercised, or crossing module boundaries. The paper's framing: evolving a complex agentic system isn't just about generating good edits, it's about knowing where those edits belong. Wang and colleagues, arXiv 2026 (157 HF community upvotes).

flashcards.prompt: According to this paper, why is 'behavior localization' a central bottleneck in evolving an agent harness?
flashcards.back_html: Modification requests describe what the system should do, but harnesses are organized by files and modules, are large and tightly coupled, and spread a given behavior across many code locations — so finding all the right places to edit is hard.

flashcards.prompt: Where did Handbook-Assisted planning show its largest gains?
flashcards.back_html: On scattered code sites, rarely executed paths, and cross-module interactions — the cases where behavior-to-code mapping is hardest to do by hand.

flashcards.prompt: Besides improving localization and edit-plan quality, what resource did Handbook-Assisted planning save?
